Why we looked at this

CAPTCHAs sit in front of account sign-ups, logins, ticket sales and contact forms. They're supposed to stop bots, but they also stop a lot of people. The W3C itself notes that a CAPTCHA without a usable alternative can make a site impossible for some disabled users to use.

The usual fix is an audio version, which mostly doesn't work. Meanwhile, bots now beat humans at many of these tests (Searles et al., 2023). Disabled users pay a high price for protection that keeps getting weaker.

We focused on the two groups most often blocked: screen-reader users and keyboard-only users, including people with motor impairments.

What the research says about audio CAPTCHAs

  • 43% Blind participants solved only 43% of audio CAPTCHAs on the first try. Bigham & Cavender, 2009
  • 5× Each one took about 51 seconds, roughly five times longer than sighted users on visual CAPTCHAs. Bigham & Cavender, 2009
  • 31% Three people fully agreed on the answer to an audio CAPTCHA only 31% of the time. Bursztein et al., 2010
